speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether the Ministry has annual data in the past five years on the average number of times when nurses in public hospitals are rostered for an afternoon shift that ends in the evening and is immediately followed by a morning shift the next day in the (i) general wards and (ii) intensive care units; (b) if so, what are they; and (c) if this data is not available, whether the Ministry intends to collect it and, if not, why not.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The rostering of nurses for shifts is managed by the hospitals which MOH does not and should not interfere.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Hospitals are operational environments, which have to address patient needs on a day-to-day basis.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Generally, healthcare workers understand and embrace this, and will cover for each other occasionally when there is an operational need, even if it means a heavier workload.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: A rigid system will result in compromising on patient care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On Mr Ng's suggestion in respect of the MOE Connect Plan, we would highlight that MOH regularly reviews and adjusts the compensation and benefits for healthcare workers to ensure that they remain competitive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We can study Mr Ng's suggestion along with other options in future reviews.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will continue to work on various ways to support, develop and retain our healthcare workers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have to take a multi-pronged approach including ensuring staff well-being, regularly reviewing compensation, attracting foreign nurses to augment our local workforce and working with families and caregivers to alleviate the load on healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I just ask again, specifically, how does MOH look into the workload of our nurses?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I ask this because, the nurse-to-patient ratio that we shared previously in Parliament of one is to four or five, seems quite far from the reality on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many nurses are sharing that they are looking after way more patients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, I do agree with the Senior Parliamentary Secretary, maybe we should not be that prescriptive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But a lot of nurses are now sharing that they only have five hours of rest between shifts and I fear not just for the nurses, but also the level of care that patients would get for someone that is overworked.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And so, I hope MOH can again review the rostering system of the hospitals and also the nurse-to-patient ratio.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: He has raised many questions in this House relating to their workload and the things that they have to address in the realities on the ground today.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But I am sure he also appreciates and understands that it is a pandemic situation that we are dealing with, and these are the realities on the ground.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have to be cognisant that we not only have to ensure that the nurses are taken care of, we also need to ensure that the patients are taken care of.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, in the light of the context that we are facing today, these are the realities on the ground that we have to acknowledge and learn how to manage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is the holistic effort and we are taking into account.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, one aspect of it is the managing of their workload.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is something that we need to leave to the hospitals and public healthcare institutions to manage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is an operational setting and setting too much rules does not help.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The reality is, even if we set the rules, the professionals, even if they are going to leave their shift, if they see a patient who is unwell, they would also still stay and still want to take care of the patient.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think this is the reality that we have to accept of the nature of the work in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Notwithstanding that, we appreciate that it is a challenging time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have explained just now and also in earlier Sittings, that we are looking at this from a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are looking to see what are the areas where we can augment the work with regard to, maybe, having technology, employing more people to help with the administrative load, looking at how we can augment the workforce with foreign nurses, looking at how we can get families and caregivers to understand where they can alleviate the load of the nurses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, these are all the efforts that are being put in place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We appreciate the concern and care, issues that Mr Louis Ng has raised, are issues that we are cognisant of and we are taking steps to try and address them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I just want to ask the Senior Parliamentary Secretary, the war for talent is felt in all industries and the healthcare industry is certainly not spared.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the review of our current policies, I want to ask Senior Parliamentary Secretary whether it includes what other countries are offering because, as I said, nurses are in short supply worldwide amongst other things.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, I hope our review takes into account who we are up against and how we can deal with them.
